analysis.evidence: אָדָם is the subject, אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ marks his wife as the direct object, and עוֹד means “again.” The next clause, וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן (“and she bore a son”), confirms the sexual sense.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־.
analysis.sense: to have sexual intercourse with someone

analysis.evidence: אָדָם stands without the article as the subject of וַיֵּדַע. The phrase עוֹד אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ recalls his earlier union with his wife. She names their son Seth and describes him as another offspring in Abel’s place, identifying Adam within this family.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun without article, prefix, or suffix.

analysis.evidence: עוֹד modifies וַיֵּדַע in וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ, “Adam again knew his wife.” It marks the recurrence of intercourse. The following clause וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן recounts the resulting birth.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected adverb with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ, אָדָם is the subject of וַיֵּדַע ‘knew’. The marked אֶת introduces its direct object, אִשְׁתּוֹ ‘his wife’, which is definite through its possessive suffix.
analysis.morphology: Unsuffixed direct-object particle, with no prefix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ, the suffix refers to Adam, who again has intercourse with his wife. She then bears a son.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular construct noun with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־וֹ.

analysis.evidence: The feminine singular verb refers to Adam’s wife. Its direct object בֵּן gives the reading “and she bore a son,” and she then names him Seth.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person feminine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix

analysis.evidence: וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן means “she bore a son.” The next clause names that son שֵׁת (Seth).
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Adam’s wife is the subject of both וַתֵּלֶד (“and she bore”) and וַתִּקְרָא (“and she named”). The phrase אֶת־שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת identifies Seth as the name she gave her son.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third-person feminine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת, “she called his name Seth,” אֶת marks שְׁמוֹ (“his name”) as the direct object of וַתִּקְרָא. The possessive suffix makes שְׁמוֹ definite, and שֵׁת gives the name she chose.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected direct-object particle, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Genesis 4:25 as an example of the existing naming sense of שֵׁם in the shem article.
draft.definition: The name by which a person is known.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:25 gives both the bearer, the newborn son, and the name his mother gives him, Seth.

patch.value: The mother calls her newborn son Seth. שְׁמוֹ means “his name,” and שֵׁת gives that name.

analysis.evidence: In וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת, “she called his name Seth,” אֶת marks שְׁמוֹ as the object of “she called.” The suffix refers back to בֵּן, “a son,” and שֵׁת supplies the name his mother gives him.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־וֹ, referring to the newborn son.
analysis.sense: name by which someone is known

analysis.evidence: וַתִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת means “she called his name Seth.” The following verb שָׁת explains the name through wordplay as the mother says that God has appointed her another offspring in Abel’s place.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: the son of Adam and his wife born after Abel’s death

analysis.evidence: כִּי introduces the mother’s reason for naming her son שֵׁת. Her words שָׁת לִי אֱלֹהִים, “God has appointed for me,” echo the name and explain it.
analysis.morphology: Unprefixed causal conjunction.

analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of שָׁת, לִי identifies the mother as the recipient, and זֶרַע אַחֵר is the object, “another offspring.” תַּחַת הֶבֶל specifies that the child takes Abel’s place. The verb שָׁת echoes the name שֵׁת and explains the mother’s choice of name.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: to appoint or provide someone as a replacement

analysis.evidence: In שָׁת לִי אֱלֹהִים זֶרַע אַחֵר, “God has appointed another offspring for me,” אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the third-person masculine singular verb שָׁת. Eve credits God with giving her another child in Abel’s place.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun with singular reference.

analysis.evidence: Eve bears a son and names him Seth. She calls him זֶרַע אַחֵר תַּחַת הֶבֶל, “another child in place of Abel.”
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute

analysis.evidence: In זֶרַע אַחֵר, “another offspring,” אַחֵר agrees with זֶרַע in gender and number. The following phrase תַּחַת הֶבֶל, “in place of Abel,” explains why Eve calls Seth another offspring.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective modifying זֶרַע, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In זֶרַע אַחֵר תַּחַת הֶבֶל, Eve describes Seth as “another offspring in place of Abel.” The following clause explains the substitution: Cain killed Abel.
analysis.morphology: Preposition without prefix or suffix, governing הֶבֶל.

analysis.evidence: תַּחַת הֶבֶל means “in place of Abel.” The following clause כִּי הֲרָגוֹ קָיִן, “because Cain killed him,” identifies Abel as the son whom Seth replaces.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun without prefix or suffix, governed by תַּחַת.

analysis.evidence: The marked כִּי introduces הֲרָגוֹ קָיִן, “Cain killed him,” explaining why Eve describes the new child as taking Abel’s place (תַּחַת הֶבֶל).
analysis.morphology: Causal conjunction without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי הֲרָגוֹ קָיִן, “because Cain killed him,” קָיִן is the subject, and the suffix ־וֹ refers to Abel (הֶבֶל).
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third masculine singular, with a third masculine singular direct-object suffix.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Cain with its etymology left open pending evidence.
draft.definition: Cain, the son of Adam and Eve and brother of Abel.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:1 names Eve’s son קַיִן. Genesis 4:2 identifies Abel as his brother and names Cain again when describing his work.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי הֲרָגוֹ קָיִן, ‘because Cain killed him,’ קָיִן is the subject of הֲרָגוֹ. The verb’s object suffix refers to הֶבֶל (Abel).
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun in the pausal form קָיִן, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abel’s brother.
